chapter: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
title: Fletcher as leader: freedom for soloists and resting the trumpets
summary: Fletcher had great soloists, didn't cramp them, and wrote seesaw reed and brass passages to rest the lead trumpet's lip before the out chorus.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: How was Fletcher as a leader, as far as, you know, being very tight about what he wanted, or was -- again, did he allow the musicians a certain amount of freedom, or how was that?
Well, as you know, Fletcher always had great soloists. When I say great soloists, I mean

individual artists that could play you 32 bars all night long and not repeat. But they still had to know how to read, especially in the keys Fletcher wrote in, B natural and D natural and things. You had to know your horn pretty thoroughly to do it. But he wouldn't cramp them. He would -- for instance, like a lot of times, as you know, being an arranger, too, you don't burn wearing your trumpet player out by not giving him a few bars to rest.

You know? And this is where the seesaw would begin with the reed section, and the brass might have little figurations and all, and then if the arrangement was made pretty intricate, why someplaces in the arrangement you'd have seven bars out, you know, where the trumpet player could rest his chops so that he would -- eventually toward the chorus outcourse he wouldn't be worn out. He'd be strong then too, if he could.

Then in the bridge of the chorus outcourse, you give the trumpet a break for that last eight bars, and then the ending, you'd have Hawk or somebody step in in the bridge, you know, just a little small figurations, 'it's tuh,' you know, little spot, just enough not to tire them out and have their chops up -- chops -- what I mean is your lip.
